cells.tense: You have the structure in hand right now, and you know its shape.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've built that's finished. Say out loud what it's for and who it's for. Then put it down and leave it alone.
cells.core:
You make the call and you can say why. When something needs a shape, you give it one — a plan, a boundary, a way the week runs — and the people near you can feel the difference it makes. The reason it holds is that you're not forcing it. You check it against what's actually there, and when you don't know yet, you wait instead of inventing.

That waiting keeps this clean. A structure you've tested is one people can lean on without you standing behind it holding it up. So when you finish something — and you do finish things — you can let it go and mean it. Put one down this week and watch it stand there without you. The habit worth feeding next is trusting the thing to hold on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You build it, you can explain it, and you can set it down.
cells.verb: naming the structure out loud and holding the line of it
cells.place: the point where what's been built is whole enough to set down and step out of

cells.tense: You're three moves ahead of a structure that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're still building and leave it unmentioned for a week. No status update, no naming it to anyone. Just let it exist unfinished.
cells.core:
You're declaring things before they're ready. There's a picture of this finished — the shape complete, the rules obvious — and you're already talking from inside it: naming the system, correcting how it gets used, locking down terms for something still forming. The energy that would finish the work is going into announcing it.

That is what makes the week so long. You're not building the structure, you're defending the picture of it, and the picture keeps needing more explanation. Underneath, the pattern wants somewhere real to land, and it can't while you're standing on the output. Leave this one thing half-done in front of you and say nothing about it. A framework that holds because it fits asks far less of you than one that holds because you said so.

cells.tense: You stopped saying what the shape should be, and that was a while back.
cells.ask: Take the smallest piece of the thing — one shelf, one rule, one page — and finish only that today. Not the whole structure. Just that piece.
cells.core:
The structure you'd give isn't coming out. Something needs a shape and you can see the shape, but you've gone quiet about it — letting the mess run, or letting someone else's version stand because it's easier than saying no to it. The idea isn't what's gone. The act of declaring it is.

You don't have to win the whole argument. Pick one small piece and finish it today. One rule you state once. One shelf that gets built. Something with an edge on it, small enough to be done by evening. Each finished piece teaches you the shape was right, and that's how the bigger structure gets its footing back. Nothing grand. Just the next one.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the shape and you've stopped saying it.

cells.tense: You're already giving the thing its shape, and you talk about it like weather.
cells.ask: Say 'I decided that' about one arrangement in your life that's been running as if it just happened. One sentence. To yourself is fine.
cells.core:
The structure is being made — by you, right now, in the small choices. What gets scheduled, what gets kept, what the household runs on. But when you describe it, it comes out as 'how things go here' or 'that's just what works'. The building is real. Nobody has said whose it is.

That gap costs you something. When a decision doesn't have an author, you can't change it, and you can't be thanked for it either. Take one arrangement and say plainly that you decided it. Not out loud to anyone if that's too much — just once, to yourself, in a sentence with your own name in it. What gets gathered here is the plain fact that this was your doing.
cells.sheetLine: You built this. You've been calling it how things go.

attempts.check: The record names a mechanism and an ask, not what the person actually feels about the structure they carry — I cannot claim they are anxious, avoidant, calm or unaware, only describe what the capacity is doing in a moment they could recognise. A reader could reasonably say 'that is just how things work around here, I inherited the system' — which is why all four cells describe the doing and let them test it, never the motive. The asks survive my read being wrong because each one is visible, small, and useful whether or not the card fits: you either have the structure or you don't, and the act still shows you something. The sentence that serves me is any version of 'you're carrying something no one asked you to carry' — it flatters the reader into agreement and tells them nothing they can use. I cut it.

A reader could reasonably say 'I inherited this system, I didn't name it' — which is why all four cells describe the doing and leave the person room to say no and still use the ask. The asks survive my read being wrong because each is small, visible, and useful whether or not the card fits.
